props.title: The Seven Year Itch

sections.content: Billy Wilder's iconic romantic comedy The Seven Year Itch (1955) defined Marilyn Monroe's screen persona and gave us cinema's most famous billowing skirt scene. The film's exploration of male fantasy and mid-life crisis influenced countless later comedies like American Beauty (1999) and Lost in Translation (2003). Tom Ewell's Richard Sherman represents the archetypal repressed 1950s businessman, while Monroe's "The Girl" embodies the era's simultaneous fascination with and fear of female sexuality. Wilder cleverly uses Richard's vivid imagination sequences to critique the male gaze decades before the term existed.

sections.content: The film's Manhattan setting and focus on summertime sexuality connects it to other New York romantic classics like Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961) and The Apartment (1960). Wilder's signature mix of cynicism and sweetness influenced later directors like Woody Allen, particularly in Manhattan (1979) and Annie Hall (1977). The film's treatment of marriage, fidelity, and fantasy laid groundwork for modern romantic comedies about commitment anxiety like Crazy, Stupid, Love (2011) and 500 Days of Summer (2009). SUBHEAD: Impact on Pop Culture and Gender Politics

While modern viewers might cringe at some dated elements, the film's self-aware humor and Monroe's knowing performance add surprising complexity. Monroe's character plays with her sex symbol status much like Bombshell (2019) later explored. The famous subway grate scene has been referenced countless times, from Insignificance (1985) to Blade Runner 2049 (2017), showing how this single image became shorthand for American sexuality and celebrity culture.
